stemBlocks.value: The quadratic function q is defined by q(x) = −3x² − 12x + 1. (a) Express q(x) in the form a(x + h)² + k, where a, h and k are constants. (b) Hence determine the maximum value of q(x). (c) State the coordinates of the maximum point of q. (d) Determine the equation of the line of symmetry of the graph of q.
Think first: The coefficient of x² is negative, so this parabola opens downwards and the completed square form will hand you a maximum, not a minimum.

contentBlocks.value: −3(x + 2)² is never positive, so q(x) is largest when (x + 2)² = 0, i.e. x = −2

solutionSteps.instruction: State the vertex and its line of symmetry.

contentBlocks.value: The vertex is (−h, k) = (−2, 13); the parabola is symmetric about the vertical line through it

strategyBlocks.value: Factor the −3 out of the two x-terms, complete the square inside the bracket, then read the vertex straight off the a(x + h)² + k form.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) q(x) = −3(x + 2)² + 13  (b) maximum value = 13  (c) maximum point (−2, 13)  (d) line of symmetry x = −2

whyThisWorks.value: Completing the square rewrites the quadratic as a single squared term plus a constant. A square is never negative, so when it is multiplied by a negative number the whole term is never positive — the expression reaches its largest value exactly when the square is zero. That single condition, x + 2 = 0, gives the x of the turning point, and the leftover constant is the turning value itself.

commonErrors.misconception: Forgetting to multiply the −4 by the factored −3, giving k = −3 instead of 13.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Forgetting to multiply the −4 by the factored −3, giving k = −3 instead of 13.

commonErrors.misconception: Reading the vertex as (2, 13) instead of (−2, 13) — the sign of h flips.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Reading the vertex as (2, 13) instead of (−2, 13) — the sign of h flips.

commonErrors.misconception: Calling 13 a minimum because the number is positive, without checking the sign of a.

examTip.value: Always check a completed square by substituting the vertex x-value back into the original expression — here q(−2) = −12 + 24 + 1 = 13 confirms it in seconds.
